newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president calls for cross-party talks.
newsitem.headline: Albania president calls for cross-party talks.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Monday invited opposition parties to join the government in talks to work out how to compensate investors left destitute by the dramatic crash of pyramid saving schemes.
But two days before the first money was due to be returned to anxious Albanians, one leading centre-left opposition group rejected Berisha's offer.

Economists believe more than $1 billion is tied up in various schemes which flourished in post-communist Albania and the collapse of part of the system ignited street protests across Europe's poorest country last month.
Berisha, founder of the ruling Democratic Party, invited all political forces to round table discussions on Tuesday to examine ways of helping hapless investors.
Albania's second opposition party, the Social Democrats, dismissed the offer as an exercise in public relations.

"Instead of discussing the deep political and economic crisis and finding the right solutions to overcome it, Berisha is assembling parties to show people how worried he is," the Social Democrat leader, Skender Gjinushi, told Reuters.
"It's really ridiculous. We refuse to participate in such an absurd scene."

It was not immediately clear if Albania's largest opposition group, the Socialists, would accept Berisha's invitation. Main anti-government parties joined forces last week to press for the resignation of the government.

Ruined depositors set fire to government buildings and offices of the Democratic Party a week ago, but calm has returned to the Balkan state as people await word on how they will be allowed to reclaim some of their savings.
A crackdown against alleged troublemakers and the threat of 15-year prison sentences for rioters deterred many would-be protestors from joining fresh demonstrations at the weekend.
The government met for several hours on Monday to discuss how to hand back some $300 million to investors from two of the pyramids whose bank assets have been frozen.

Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told state television after the meeting that investors from the Xhaferri and Populli funds could go to state-owned banks on Wednesday to receive some of their trapped savings.
He said it had not yet been decided what percentage of their investments would be returned.
Staff at Tirana's main banks were plouging through ragged documents and receipts to determine how much to pay depositors.
Five national funds have failed since November but only two had bank assets. Berisha has warned that investors in the other three pyramids will get no compensation.

Albania's largest investment firm, Vefa Holdings, slashed salaries for its administrative staff by 50 percent on Monday and reduced monthly interest payments to three percent from five. Its directors deny that they operate a pyramid scheme under which new deposits fund earlier interest bills.
In January, Vefa prevented people from withdrawing their invested capital. It is not known exactly how much money has been sunk into the company.

"As far as I'm concerned it has already collapsed. If the government wants, it can survive for a little while, but not for much longer," said a financial consultant who advises the World Bank, declining to be named.
